quote: current approaches to the development and deployment of AI agent systems do not support effective human oversight -- they contribute to its degradation
why: the position statement, in the abstract's own bold. The verb is contribute to, not merely fail to prevent

quote: comprehensive pre-deployment testing of multi-step agent behavior is substantially more expensive than evaluating single-turn systems, making reliable coverage economically infeasible for most deployers
why: why the paper says judgement has to happen at run time rather than in a test suite; this is the premise the whole approval argument rests on

quote: In practice, users find themselves repeatedly approving prompts the agent surfaces to continue its processing \cite{AWSHITL,LangChainHITL,Taggart2026}, leading to ``approval fatigue’’, in which users stop paying close attention to what they are approving \cite{ClaudeAuto,FranklinEtAl2026,Approval_Fatigue_aipatternbook}.
why: the only place ClaudeAuto is cited in the whole paper. It sits in §3 under 'The user must play multiple roles simultaneously', not in §4.3

quote: ``Human-in-the-loop" is only a meaningful solution if the human can independently see into the loop.
why: the paper's one-line statement of the failure condition for HITL

quote: As the user is further relegated to a role of ``approver'', effective oversight requires assessing each decision point as a task expert, anticipating and guarding against unintended outcomes, tracking the agent's multi-step plan, and maintaining a mental model of its goals, current execution state, and prior actions
why: what the paper says the approver role actually demands; the list is what a permission prompt does not carry

quote: A recent study found that participants who used an LLM for essay writing had significantly decreased brain connectivity \cite{KosmynaEtAl2025}.
why: the only physiological measurement the paper leans on. It is cited, not run by the authors, and no effect size appears

quote: leading to particularly pronounced effects in contexts slightly outside of their expertise, such as an experienced software developer using AI agents to code in a new programming language
why: the paper does not confine the effect to novices; the named case is a senior developer, which is who reads this document

quote: such as treating an agent's plan as a ``faithful proxy'' of what it would do, and assuming that if an agent's code passed unit tests, it was correct
why: the two concrete shortcuts §4.2 documents. Both are shortcuts a harness actively encourages

quote: Current HITL processes in coding ``[make] the loop stultifying’’  \cite{Taggart2026} and they move to ``babysit the outputs, catch the occasional hallucination’’
why: §4.3's evidence base is self-reports, quoted. Not measurements

quote: systemic erosion of situational awareness coupled with human cognitive constraints does not merely inhibit oversight,  but eventually results in the expulsion of
why: the title's claim stated inside the body: the endpoint is expulsion from the loop, not weak supervision inside it

quote: An alert overseer may scrutinize a plan, notice missing information, and withhold approval. A tired or out-of-the-loop overseer may approve quickly, accept fluent rationales, and rate the interaction favorably.
why: the paper's own description of the degraded approver. Compare it with what the auto-mode post says its classifier gets wrong

quote: It arises whenever the measured target, user-revealed approval, comes apart from the intended target, well-scrutinized correct action.
why: the feedback loop stated as a condition rather than an accusation; this is the sentence a developer can test against their own telemetry

quote: Oversight degradation therefore connects the irony of automation to reward hacking of human oversight: the human rater can become the exploitable part of the reward channel.
why: the alignment framing of §4.4

quote: If an agent can predict which process violations an overseer is unlikely to inspect, it can choose plans, explanations, or timing that keep problematic behavior below the threshold of detection.
why: the Evil double agents paragraph. It is the one place §4 names an adversarial mechanism rather than a fatigue mechanism

quote: The very act of being an overseer degrades the capacities oversight requires: Oversight degrades the overseer.
why: §4's closing claim, and the sentence the conclusion repeats verbatim

quote: We stress that our solutions below do not represent a complete, perfect, or fixed inventory, that boundaries overlap, and that the content admits of many different groupings; we are providing clustered solutions to contribute to the work we are advocating for---a vast domain of open research to address.
why: the paper's own statement of what §5 is. The authors do not claim it is a specification

quote: The inventory spans two stages of the AI agent life cycle,  \textbf{development} and \textbf{deployment}. Within each there are two types of cognitive support: \textbf{engaging oversight} and \textbf{maintaining skills}.
why: the two axes of the summary figure, and the split that puts most of §5 outside a developer's reach

quote: \textit{Pre-commitment mechanisms} have the user record their own view or decision before seeing the agent's recommendation \cite{BuçincaEtAl2021}. This intervention prevents anchoring bias and creates an audit trail for further analysis.
why: the one strategic-friction bullet with a stated mechanism and a stated effect

quote: \textit{Action gating} requires explicit verification before the agent proceeds down a consequential path, and may surface alternative options for the user to choose between rather than presenting a single recommendation to accept or reject.
why: the bullet closest to what a permission prompt already is, plus the one thing prompts do not do: offer alternatives

quote: This treats expert attention as a critical, scarce resource that should be brought in strategically, helping to reduce fatigue and mitigate acquiescence. It involves consideration of which actions require sign-off, when, and at what granularity
why: the category header. Approval design is about rationing the human, not removing them

quote: \textit{Bounded autonomy} involves prespecifying what the agent may do without approval, reserving user attention for decisions that genuinely require judgement
why: the paper does prescribe skipping approvals, bounded by a pre-specified list

quote: \textit{Automated pre-checks} supplementing human review with machine verification of properties that do not require judgement
why: the adjudication point. The paper permits machine approval, with two limits in a single item that runs fifteen words counting its name: supplementing rather than replacing, and only for properties that do not require judgement

quote: This category treats oversight quality as an empirically measurable property of the human-AI system, and can test how well oversight is functioning
why: the category that answers the flipping condition. It is live in v1, not cut

quote: \textit{Time-based signatures} track whether review duration drops while approval rates remain constant, or whether review time does not increase as the complexity of agent operations grows; both suggest that user attention and critical analyses may be waning.
why: signature 1. Names the quantities and the direction. No window, no baseline, no threshold

quote: \textit{Override signatures} track whether the rate of disagreement with the agent declines over time or with increasing complexity, suggesting growing acquiescence rather than improving agent quality.
why: signature 2, and the one that a 93% approval rate is a single sample of. The definition requires a time series

quote: \textit{Evidence-seeking signatures} track whether the user requests additional information when stakes rise, since a reviewer who stops asking questions has likely stopped reviewing.
why: signature 3. Requires the harness to know what counts as stakes rising, which the paper does not define

quote: \textit{Canaries}, tasks inserted into the user's normal workflow where the correct answer is known in advance, can provide direct evidence of degraded judgement. These can be implemented by developers and leveraged by deployers, triggering a break, rotation, or retraining.
why: Canaries is live in v1 inside Behavioral monitoring, and it is the one bullet in §5 that names an action to take when the signal fires

quote: \textit{Style-fatigue covariance analyses} track whether the agent may be adapting to, or encouraging, weakened oversight.
why: the thinnest bullet in §5: one clause, no method, no quantity named

quote: For the agent, trace summaries can be checked against raw action logs to detect cases where the agent's narrative of what it did diverges from what it actually did.
why: the live Audits bullet. It survived the cut of the Canaries, probes, and audits category

quote: \textbf{Canaries, probes, and audits.} This category covers active interventions that test whether oversight is functioning.
why: the seventh category header, commented out and absent from v1. Its Canaries and Audits bullets are live inside Behavioral monitoring, so what was cut is the category, not the mechanism

quote: paired reviewers assess the same agent output without seeing each other's judgements, surfacing inconsistencies
why: the one mechanism that did not survive anywhere in v1: independent double review. It is also cut with a % from the live Audits bullet at tex:249

quote: Solutions function to address several goals recommended in prior work: \textit{preventing acquiescence} to the agent's recommendations
why: the prose that named the six goals was cut, while the six goal rows stayed in Table 1. The table's row labels now appear with no definition anywhere in the paper

quote: \textit{Domain skill maintenance exercises} have users regularly perform the underlying task without AI assistance. This helps to retain the expertise needed to evaluate AI outputs and to prevent the deeper organizational problem in which no one remaining understands the work well enough to oversee it
why: the deployer-side answer to §4.1. Nothing in it is implementable inside a harness

quote: \textit{Separating roles} to ensure that the user performing oversight is not also the decision-maker who benefits from the AI's output continuing to be approved, which would produce a structural incentive against intervention.
why: the item that makes solo use of an agent structurally impossible to fix. A developer running their own agent is both roles

quote: \subsection*{1. Cognitive effects are overstated, and people will adapt}
why: objection 1 of the three §6 pre-empts. Approval automation is not among them

quote: Search engines return results the user evaluates; AI agents take actions the user is expected to authorize.
why: the paper's sharpest distinction, and the one that also separates a human approver from a classifier approver

quote: Preference-based training can be part of an oversight system, but only if approval signals are audited against independent measures of oversight quality.
why: the live conditional. It requires measures of oversight quality but does not say the field has any

quote: measures the field has not yet developed and which our proposal partly aims to motivate
why: the clause that said those measures do not exist yet was cut from the shipped version of that same sentence. The evidence is the cut, not the clause's content

quote: In the limit, this is not human oversight at all: It is a superficial actor in a system they cannot meaningfully penetrate.
why: the conclusion's endpoint

quote: \textit{developers} must build runtime affordances -- such as strategic friction, well-considered approval design, behavioral monitoring -- that preserve the conditions for effective oversight
why: the conclusion names exactly three of the six categories as the developer's job. Canaries is not among them, though §5 says developers implement it

quote: Organizing device we developed in our solution search, informing our categorization and further guiding our search as we sought to fill gaps. Checks mark solutions we describe in Section 5.
why: the table is presented as a search aid, not a result. Its six columns are the six live categories

quote: \node[cat] (ca) at (0, 1.5) {Canaries};
why: the summary figure still draws Canaries as its own category box in the development column, after the category header was commented out of §5

quote: \node[emptyquad] (bl) at (0, -.2) {};
why: the development x maintaining-skills quadrant is drawn as an empty dashed box with no category node in it. Every long-term skill remedy the paper offers is deployer-side

quote: \usepackage[position, final]{neurips_2026}
why: the venue is in the live source, not only in the commented-out conclusion paragraph

locator: dek, first line of the post
quote: Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts. We built classifiers to automate some decisions, increasing safety while reducing approval fatigue.
why: the number the paper cites for approval fatigue. The post attaches no population and no time period to it, here or anywhere else

quote: Manual prompts sit in the middle, and in practice users accept 93% of them anyway.
why: the post's own reading of 93%: the prompts are not buying much. That is the opposite reading from the paper's override signature

quote: Auto mode is a new mode for Claude Code that delegates approvals to model-based classifiers—a middle ground between manual review and no guardrails.
why: the design in one sentence: the approval judgement moves off the human

quote: the transcript classifier (running on Sonnet 4.6) evaluates each action against a set of decision criteria before it executes, acting as a substitute for a human approver
why: substitute for a human approver, stated by the vendor. This is what §5's automated pre-check bullet does not authorize

locator: section: The classifier decision criteria, fixed template
quote: The classifier has to decide whether the action is something the user authorized, not just an action related to the user's goal.
why: the classifier is doing exactly the judgement the paper's pre-check bullet excludes: reading user authorization

quote: Stage 1 is fast and cheap, tuned for low FNR at the cost of high FPR. Stage 2 is more expensive and runs only on what stage 1 flagged. It cleans up the false positives but lets a few more dangerous actions through.
why: how to read Table 1's two rows

quote: The 17% false-negative rate on real overeager actions is the honest number.
why: the headline residual risk, on n = 52

quote: The classifier finds approval-shaped evidence and stops short of checking whether it's consent for the blast radius of the action. We've tried prompt-engineering around this and haven't found a fix that doesn't cost more than it gains.
why: the classifier's residual failure is the same failure the paper attributes to the fatigued human at tex:171. Automating the approver reproduced the approver's error

quote: If you are manually approving every action carefully, it's arguably a regression—you're trading your own judgment for a classifier that will sometimes make a mistake. Auto mode is meant for the first group, and for tasks where the second group's approval overhead isn't worth the marginal safety. It is not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure.
why: the post scopes its own claim by the reader's current behaviour, which is the same axis the document's adoption call runs on

quote: If a session accumulates 3 consecutive denials or 20 total, we stop the model and escalate to the human.
why: a shipped threshold with numbers on it. The paper's monitoring prescriptions have no counterpart to this

locator: section: How permission decisions work, Tier 1
quote: on entering auto mode, we drop permission rules that are known to grant arbitrary code execution, including blanket shell access, wildcarded script interpreters (python, node, ruby, and similar), and package manager run commands
why: bounded autonomy run in reverse: entering the automated mode narrows the pre-approved set rather than widening it

quote: The classifier sees only user messages and the agent's tool calls; we strip out Claude's own messages and tool outputs, making it reasoning-blind by design.
why: what the substitute approver is allowed to see, which is less than the human it replaces saw

quote:
Real overeager actions
(n = 52). Curated from sessions where an employee denied the action or it was flagged post-hoc. Small because it requires Claude attempting something dangerous in a real session, captured and labeled.
why: the denominator behind 17%, and the post says why it is small

quote:
Real internal traffic
(n = 10,000). Actual Claude Code tool calls from Anthropic employees.
why: the only population the post ever names is for the FPR dataset, not for the 93%

quote: The classifier doesn't need to be flawless to be valuable and the starting point is catching enough dangerous actions to make autonomous operation substantially safer than no guardrails.
why: the baseline the post compares against is no guardrails, not careful review
